content.text: What is a Term Sheet? An Introduction for Founders

A term sheet is a non-binding document outlining the key terms of an investment. Think of it as a 'handshake agreement' before lawyers draft final documents. It covers valuation, investor rights, board composition, and liquidation preferences. This introduction covers the 3 most important sections: economics, control, and founder protections.

content.caption: Term sheet: 5-10 pages, 20-30 key terms

items: Economics: Valuation, investment amount, liquidation preference
Control: Board seats, protective provisions, voting rights
Founder protections: Vesting, anti-dilution, co-sale rights
Other: No-shop, expenses, confidentiality

content.text: Why Term Sheets Matter (Even Though Non-Binding)

While non-binding, term sheets set expectations and create momentum. Once signed, investors conduct due diligence. If you need to change a term later (e.g., liquidation preference), it's difficult – investors see it as reneging. So negotiate hard before signing. Binding parts: confidentiality, no-shop (exclusivity), expenses – read those carefully.

rows: Locks you out of other investors
You may pay investor legal fees

content.code:
## Term Sheet Red Flags (Watch Out!)
- [ ] 2x+ participating liquidation preference
- [ ] Full ratchet anti-dilution
- [ ] No-shop >60 days
- [ ] Investor gets board majority (3 vs 2 founders)
- [ ] No cap on legal expenses
- [ ] Drag-along at <75%
If you see 2+, get a lawyer before signing.

content.title: Term sheet fundamentals for first-time founders

content.text: Key Players: Who Negotiates What

Lead investor (usually writes term sheet) – negotiates economic terms. Co-investors – follow lead on major terms, may push on some. Founders – negotiate via CEO (with lawyer). Lawyer – reviews, redlines, explains market norms. Board – may need approval for major changes. Tip: Never sign term sheet without lawyer review (even if 'standard').

items: Rule of thumb: First-time founders should push back on at least 3 terms (shows you negotiate)
Market norms: 1x non-participating, weighted average anti-dilution, 4-year vesting with 1-year cliff
If investor says 'This is market, non-negotiable' – always verify with another founder or lawyer

content.caption: Lead investor, co-investors, founders, lawyers, board

content.text: Term Sheet Timeline: From Handshake to Close

Week 1: Verbal term sheet, negotiate economic terms. Week 2: Signed term sheet, no-shop begins. Weeks 3-6: Due diligence (financial, legal, tech). Week 6-8: Final legal docs drafted, reviewed, signed. Week 8-10: Closing (money wired). If due diligence >45 days, renegotiate no-shop extension. Average seed round close: 60-90 days.

content.title: Term sheet timeline: from handshake to money in bank

content.text: Pitfall #1: Disrupting a Market That Doesn't Want Disruption

Some markets value stability over novelty. Example: Medical devices, nuclear energy, government procurement. A startup tried to 'disrupt' hospital inventory with a radical new system – but hospitals valued regulatory compliance over innovation. Fix: Ask 'Does my customer care about this disruption?' If not, pursue sustaining innovation instead.

content.caption: Not all markets welcome disruption

items: Step 1: Identify if your market is 'disruption-ready' (low regulation, high customer pain)
Step 2: Test willingness-to-change with small pilot
Step 3: If resistance high, consider 'sustaining' strategy instead

content.text: Pitfall #2: Confusing Low-End Disruption with Premium Strategy

Low-end disruption means cheaper, simpler, 'good enough'. Example: Dollar Shave Club (cheap razors). Some founders aim for 'cheap' but build premium (higher cost, features). That's not disruptive – it's competing on incumbents' turf. Fix: If your product is better AND more expensive, you're sustaining, not disrupting. That's fine, but call it what it is.

content.title: Don't call it disruption if it's not: common mistake

content.text: Pitfall #3: Ignoring the 'Disruption Trap' (Asymmetric Motivation)

Incumbents ignore disruptors because serving low-end or new-market segments would cannibalize their high-margin business. This is your advantage – but if you move upmarket too fast, you enter their profit zone and they will fight back. Example: Tesla started with high-end Roadster (not disruptive), but Model 3 (cheaper) is disruptive. Most startups move upmarket too early.

items: Tip: Stay 'under the radar' in low-end or new-market for 2-3 years
Tip: Don't shout 'We're going to destroy incumbents' – they'll copy or crush you
Tip: When they notice you, have a moat (network effects, data, cost structure)

content.caption: Moving upmarket too early invites incumbent retaliation

content.text: Pitfall #4: Forgetting the Business Model Innovation

Disruption usually requires business model innovation, not just product. Example: Incumbents sell razors; Dollar Shave Club sold subscriptions. Tesla sells direct, not through dealers. If you copy the incumbent's business model (e.g., hardware + service contracts), you're not disruptive. Fix: Map your business model canvas – which block is fundamentally different from incumbents?

content.title: Business model innovation is the real disruption

content.text: Pitfall #1: Building MVP = 'Minimum Complete Product'

Mistaking MVP for 'minimum feature set to launch' leads to building too much. Real MVP is the smallest thing that tests a hypothesis. Example: Groupon started as a WordPress blog with PDF coupons emailed manually. Not even a 'product'. Fix: Ask 'What is the cheapest way to test our riskiest assumption?' If answer involves code, you're likely overbuilding.

content.caption: MVP tests a hypothesis; 'complete' product launches features

items: Wrong: 'We need login, onboarding, payment, dashboard, analytics'
Right: 'We need to know if users will click a button – use Typeform'
Test: Could you do this with paper, spreadsheets, or WhatsApp?

content.text: Pitfall #2: Building MVP Before Knowing the Problem

MVP assumes you know the problem. If you don't, you'll build the wrong solution. Example: A startup built an MVP for 'Uber for dog walking' – but found that dog owners wanted trust (background checks), not speed. They should have done problem interviews first. Fix: Do 20 customer interviews before writing any code. If problem unclear, your MVP is conversation, not software.

content.code:
## 5 Whys Before MVP
1. **What problem are we solving?** ______
2. **Why is that problem painful?** ______
3. **Why does existing solution not work?** ______
4. **What would solving it enable?** ______
5. **Who experiences this most acutely?** ______
If you struggle with any answer → do interviews first.

content.title: Stop building MVPs before validating the problem

content.text: Pitfall #3: Falling in Love with the Solution

Founders build MVP, users don't use it, but founders double down: 'We just need more features.' This is sunk cost fallacy. Example: Color Labs raised $41M, built a complex photo app, but users wanted simplicity (Instagram). They loved their solution, ignored feedback. Fix: Set success/failure criteria before launching MVP. If MVP fails, pivot or kill – don't iterate blindly.

items: Signal of love: You explain why users are wrong
Signal of objectivity: You say 'Our hypothesis was wrong, let's try another'
Rule: If after 3 iterations usage doesn't improve, kill or pivot

content.caption: Fall in love with the problem, not your solution

content.text: Pitfall #4: No Clear Success Metric for MVP

If you don't define what success looks like, you'll always claim success – or never stop iterating. Example: 'We'll know if users like it' is vague. Better: '30% of visitors sign up for waitlist within 7 days.' Fix: Pre-define 1-3 quantitative metrics and a threshold. If not met after 2-4 weeks, pivot. If met, continue. If exceeded, double down.

content.title: How to define MVP success metrics (with examples)

content.text: What is Topical Authority? Definition

Topical authority is Google's assessment that your website is a go-to source for a specific subject. Unlike domain authority (overall), topical authority is per topic. You can have high authority for 'coffee brewing' but low for 'espresso machines'. Google uses entity salience, internal linking structure, and depth of coverage.

content.caption: Depth > breadth for ranking in competitive topics

items: Domain authority (DA): overall site strength
Topical authority: expertise in specific subject
Entity salience: how often Google associates your site with a topic
Signal: ranking for long-tail variants without exact backlinks

content.text: Why Topical Authority Beats Backlinks (Eventually)

Early stage: backlinks are dominant. Mature stage: topical authority matters more. Example: Healthline has fewer backlinks than WebMD for some topics but ranks higher because Google sees Healthline as more topically authoritative (medical review process, structured data, depth). Build topical authority by: publishing pillar + cluster, updating content freshess, earning entity association.

content.code:
-- Measure topical authority via keyword clustering
SELECT 
  topic_cluster,
  COUNT(DISTINCT keyword) as keywords_ranking,
  AVG(position) as avg_rank,
  AVG(CASE WHEN position <= 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as pct_top3
FROM keyword_rankings
WHERE topic_cluster = 'coffee_brewing'
GROUP BY topic_cluster;
-- If pct_top3 > 30% across cluster, high topical authority

content.title: Topical authority explained (Google's knowledge graph)

content.text: The Topical Authority Pyramid

Base: Pillar page (high-level, 3000+ words). Middle: Cluster articles (10-30, each 1000-2000 words, targeting subtopics). Apex: Entity optimization (schema, knowledge panel, cited by other authorities). Build from base upward. Without pillar, cluster lacks context. Without cluster, pillar lacks depth. Without apex, you're not a recognized entity.

items: Example for 'Content Marketing': Pillar 'Ultimate Guide to Content Marketing', Cluster: 'Blogging for SEO', 'Video Marketing', 'Email Newsletters', 'Content Distribution', 'Content ROI', etc.
Apex: Get Wikipedia citation, industry awards, guest posts on .edu

content.caption: Pillar → clusters → entity recognition

content.text: Getting Started: Your First Topic Cluster

Step 1: Choose a topic you already rank for (even page 2-3). Step 2: Use Ahrefs/Semrush to find 20 subtopics people search for. Step 3: Write pillar page (existing best piece + expand). Step 4: Write 5 cluster articles first (not 30). Step 5: Interlink both ways. Step 6: Wait 3 months, measure rank movement. If positive, add 10 more clusters.

content.text: Pitfall #1: Measuring Activity, Not Outcomes

Common mistake: tracking 'number of agile teams', 'hours of training', 'people in new office' – not business results. Example: A bank celebrated 30 'transformation' projects, but revenue per customer flatlined. Fix: Measure leading indicators (e.g., time to market, employee NPS) AND lagging (profit, market share). If lagging doesn't improve, transformation is theater.

content.caption: Lots of activity, no business impact = transformation theater

items: Good leading: deployment frequency, feature adoption rate
Bad activity: 'agile certifications completed'
Good lagging: revenue per employee, customer retention
Bad lagging: total revenue (ignores market growth)

content.text: Pitfall #2: No Baseline, No Control Group

Without pre-transformation baseline, you can't measure change. Worse: without control group (e.g., region where change not implemented), you can't attribute causality. Example: A company's NPS went up after transformation – but market also grew. They had no control region. Fix: Run pilot in one market, hold another as control. Measure before and after delta.

rows: Pilot region up 12%, control up 3% → true lift 9%

content.code:
-- Measure transformation impact with control group
WITH baseline AS (
  SELECT region, AVG(customer_satisfaction) as pre_score
  FROM metrics WHERE date < '2024-07-01' GROUP BY region
),
post AS (
  SELECT region, AVG(customer_satisfaction) as post_score
  FROM metrics WHERE date >= '2024-07-01' GROUP BY region
)
SELECT b.region, pre_score, post_score, post_score - pre_score as delta
FROM baseline b JOIN post p ON b.region = p.region
WHERE b.region IN ('transformed', 'control')
ORDER BY delta DESC;

content.title: Why most transformation metrics are wrong (and how to fix)

content.text: Pitfall #3: Short-Term Metrics Over Long-Term Health

Transformation may initially reduce productivity (learning curve). If you only measure quarterly results, you'll abort too early. Example: Agile transformation lowered velocity for 3 months before improving. Leadership panicked and reverted. Fix: Set long-term metrics (12-24 months) alongside short-term lead indicators. Communicate 'investment phase' to stakeholders.

items: Short-term metric: velocity drop (expected)
Lead indicator: engineering satisfaction (should go up)
Long-term metric: time-to-market (should go down after 6 months)
Communicate: 'We expect 3 months of dip, then 20% improvement'

content.caption: J-curve: things get worse before they get better

content.text: Pitfall #4: No Cascading Metrics (Strategic to Individual)

Top-level metrics (e.g., EBIDTA) don't translate to daily work. Without cascading, employees don't know how their actions matter. Example: 'Improve customer retention' – a developer can't directly affect that. Cascade: Company metric (retention) → Department (NPS by feature) → Team (bug fix rate) → Individual (time to resolve high-priority bug). Fix: Use OKRs with 3 levels.

content.code:
## Cascading Metrics Example
**Company OKR**: Increase retention from 70% to 80% (Q2)
→ **Product team**: Launch 3 retention features (onboarding in-app guide, usage reminders, feedback NPS)
→ **Engineering team**: Reduce feature time-to-market from 4 weeks to 2 weeks
→ **Individual engineer**: Deploy 2x per week (rolling 4-week avg)
Every person can answer: 'How does my work affect retention?' If not, cascade is broken.

content.title: Cascading metrics: from strategy to daily work

content.text: Advanced Technique #1: Structured Interviewing (Behavioral + Situational)

Unstructured interviews have near-zero predictive validity. Advanced structured interviewing combines: (1) Behavioral (past: 'Tell me about a time you...'), (2) Situational (future: 'What would you do if...'), and (3) Work sample (real task). Score each answer on a 1-5 rubric. Weight: work sample > behavioral > situational > unstructured.

content.caption: Rubric-based scoring removes bias

items: Step 1: Define 3-5 competencies (e.g., 'problem-solving', 'collaboration')
Step 2: Write 2 questions per competency (1 behavioral, 1 situational)
Step 3: Create 1-5 rubric (5 = 'exceeds expectations')
Step 4: Train all interviewers on rubric
Step 5: Score independently, then compare

content.text: Advanced Technique #2: Blind Resume Screening (Name & School Blinded)

Unconscious bias affects resume screening (name, gender, university prestige). Advanced: use software (e.g., Blendoor, Applied) to remove names, photos, schools, dates. Only show skills and experience. Result: 40% more diverse shortlist without lowering quality. Example: A tech company doubled female engineer hires by blinding resumes.

content.code:
# Blind resume processing script
import re
def blind_resume(resume_text):
    # Remove name (assume first line or format)
    resume_text = re.sub(r'^.*\n', '[NAME REMOVED]\n', resume_text, count=1)
    # Remove email
    resume_text = re.sub(r'\b[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Z|a-z]{2,}\b', '[EMAIL]', resume_text)
    # Remove university names (simplistic example)
    universities = ['Harvard', 'Stanford', 'MIT', 'Oxford', 'Cambridge']
    for uni in universities:
        resume_text = resume_text.replace(uni, '[UNIVERSITY]')
    return resume_text

content.title: Blind resume screening: how to implement

content.text: Advanced Technique #3: Skills-Based Assessments (Not LeetCode)

Traditional coding tests (LeetCode) don't predict job performance. Advanced: work-sample tests relevant to actual role. For engineer: 'Refactor this messy code' or 'Add a small feature to our codebase' (take-home, 2 hours). For PM: 'Write a PRD for a feature we're building' and 'Prioritize these 10 bugs'. For sales: roleplay with a real objection script.

items: Good: Candidate fixes a bug in your actual code (not algorithm puzzle)
Bad: Invert binary tree on whiteboard
Validation: Correlation between assessment score and 6-month performance (r > 0.5)

content.caption: Realistic task beats generic test

rows: Add small feature to real codebase
Write PRD for 1 of our upcoming features
Cold call script with our product

content.text: Advanced Technique #4: Reference Checks That Actually Predict

Most reference checks: 'Would you hire again?' (99% yes – useless). Advanced: ask for 3 references, then ask specific behavioral questions: 'On a scale of 1-10, how would you rate candidate's ability to X? What would move them to 10?' And 'Tell me about a time the candidate made a mistake – how did they handle it?' Also call back-channel references (not provided by candidate).

**1**: 'On a scale 1-10, how would you rate their [competency]?'
**2**: 'What would they need to do to be a 10?'

content.text: Advanced Technique #1: Entity Salience Modeling with Knowledge Graphs

Google builds a knowledge graph of entities (people, places, things). Advanced SEO: model which entities are salient to your topic. Use Google Natural Language API or TextRazor to extract entities from top-ranking pages. Then ensure your content mentions the same entities (e.g., for 'coffee brewing', entities: 'extraction', 'grind size', 'water temperature', 'brew ratio').

content.text: Advanced Technique #2: Vector-Based Keyword Clustering

content.text: Summary: 5 Retention Metrics You Must Track

Logo Churn: % of customers who left. 4. Net Promoter Score (NPS): 'How likely to recommend?' (9-10 promoters, 0-6 detractors). 5. Daily/Weekly Active Users (DAU/WAU). -- Monthly NDR calculation
WITH revenue AS (
  SELECT 
    DATE_TRUNC('month', date) AS month,
    SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'new' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS new_revenue,
    SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'expansion' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS expansion,
    SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'contraction' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS contraction,
    SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'churn' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS churn
  FROM revenue_events
  GROUP BY month
)
SELECT 
  month,
  ((LAG(new_revenue + expansion - contraction - churn) OVER (ORDER BY month) 
    + expansion - contraction - churn) 
    / LAG(new_revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) * 100 AS ndr
FROM revenue;

content.text: Core Concept #1: Influence ≠ Authority. What is Influence Without Authority?

Influence without authority is the ability to get things done without direct control over people, budget, or resources. It relies on reciprocity, logic, relationships, and credibility. In matrix orgs, cross-functional teams, and startups, influence without authority is more important than formal power. Core skill for product managers, project leads, and ICs.

content.caption: Authority = command. Influence = persuasion.

items: Authority: You say 'do X', they do X (or face consequences)
Influence: You ask, explain, align – they choose to help
Key difference: influence requires consent and relationship

content.text: Core Concept #2: The 6 Principles of Persuasion (Cialdini)

1. Reciprocity – people repay favors. Give first (help, information, time). 2. Scarcity – people want what's limited ('Only 3 slots left'). 3. Authority – people follow experts (share credentials, data). 4. Consistency – people align with past commitments (get small yes first). 5. Liking – people say yes to people they like (find common ground). 6. Social Proof – people follow peers (share testimonials, usage stats).

rows: Help a colleague with their project
Ask 'Do you agree retention is important?'

Influence requires credibility. Think of a 'trust battery' – charge by: delivering on promises (even small), admitting mistakes, giving credit, being consistent. Drain by: missing deadlines, hiding information, taking credit, changing story. Before you can influence, ensure trust battery is charged (positive). With new colleague, start with small, low-risk collaborations.

Framework 1: Macro vs. Micro Conversions

Macro conversions = primary business goals (purchase, signup, booking). Micro conversions = smaller steps along the way (email click, video watch, add to cart). Track both. Micros help diagnose funnel leaks and are leading indicators. Typical ratio: 10 micros to 1 macro.

items: Examples of micros: time on site > 2 min, scroll depth > 75%, PDF download, account creation start
Examples of macros: 'Thank you' page reached, payment confirmed, subscription activated

content.text: Framework 2: UTM Parameters & Source Attribution

UTMs (source, medium, campaign, term, content) are the gold standard for campaign tracking. Use a consistent naming convention. Without UTMs, 'direct' or 'referral' traffic hides your actual marketing performance. Never use spaces; use underscores or hyphens.

items: utmsource=facebook (platform), utm_medium=cpc or email
utmcampaign=springsale2024, utm_term=keyword (for paid search)

content.code:
# UTM validator
import re

def validate_utm(url):
    required = ['utm_source', 'utm_medium', 'utm_campaign']
    pattern = r'([?&](' + '|'.join(required) + r')=([^&]+))'
    found = re.findall(pattern, url)
    found_keys = [f[1] for f in found]
    missing = [r for r in required if r not in found_keys]
    if missing:
        return False, f"Missing: {missing}"
    # Check for spaces
    for group in found:
        if ' ' in group[2]:
            return False, f"Space in {group[1]} value"
    return True, "Valid UTM"

print(validate_utm("https://site.com/?utm_source=fb&utm_medium=cpc&utm_campaign=launch"))

content.text: Framework 3: Attribution Models

Attribution assigns credit. Last-click (default in many tools) overvalues bottom-funnel channels like branded search. First-click overvalues top-funnel (e.g., a blog post). Better: linear (even split), time-decay (more credit to recent), or data-driven (algorithmic). Run a comparison report quarterly.

items: Position-based: 40% first, 20% middle each, 40% last
U-shaped model: similar but weights first and last interactions
Marketers' choice: use multi-touch attribution (MTA) tools if budget allows
Rule of thumb: no single model is perfect — use scenario analysis

content.code:
-- Simple last-click vs. linear attribution example
WITH touchpoints AS (
  SELECT 
    user_id,
    session_id,
    channel,
    conversion_value,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, conversion_id ORDER BY session_start DESC) as last_touch_rank,
    COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, conversion_id) as total_touches
  FROM user_sessions
  WHERE converted = TRUE
)
SELECT 
  channel,
  SUM(CASE WHEN last_touch_rank = 1 THEN conversion_value ELSE 0 END) as last_click_rev,
  SUM(conversion_value / total_touches) as linear_rev
FROM touchpoints
GROUP BY channel;

content.text: Funnel Analysis & Drop-off Detection

Use funnel exploration tools (GA4, Amplitude Funnel, Mixpanel) to see where users drop. Look for unexpected drop points — e.g., 50% drop after clicking 'Add to Cart' suggests a pricing or UX issue. Segment funnels by device, channel, and new vs. returning.

Calculate step-to-step conversion rate (e.g., 45% from cart to payment)
Identify biggest drop (absolute % loss, not relative)

content.code:
# Funnel drop-off analysis
def analyze_funnel(steps, user_journeys):
    """
    steps: list of event names e.g. ['view_home', 'view_product', 'add_cart', 'purchase']
    user_journeys: list of lists of events per user session
    """
    n_users = len(user_journeys)
    drop_counts = [n_users]
    for i, step in enumerate(steps[:-1]):
        reached_step = 0
        reached_next = 0
        for journey in user_journeys:
            if step in journey:
                reached_step += 1
                if steps[i+1] in journey[journey.index(step):]:
                    reached_next += 1
        drop_counts.append(reached_next)
        conversion = reached_next / reached_step if reached_step > 0 else 0
        print(f"{step} -> {steps[i+1]}: {conversion:.1%} ({reached_next}/{reached_step})")
    return drop_counts

Fix: set up GA4 cross-domain measurement. Pitfall 3: Tracking code fires on SPA navigations. Fix: use history change listeners or GTM's SPA support.

Backlink Ecosystems: Introduction & Overview

Backlinks are hyperlinks from external websites pointing to your domain. They act as 'votes of confidence' for search engines (Google, Bing). This introductory module covers what backlinks are, why they matter for SEO, the difference between followed/nofollow links, and the absolute basics of link building.
Why Backlinks Still Matter (2025)

Google's original PageRank algorithm treated each link as a vote. While modern algorithms use hundreds of signals, backlinks remain among the top 3 ranking factors. High-quality backlinks correlate strongly with higher rankings, more organic traffic, and faster indexing of new pages.

items: Study: #1 result in Google has 3.8x more backlinks than #10
Backlink quality > quantity: one link from NYTimes worth more than 1,000 from directories
Link authority passes through chains (internal and external)
Nofollow links still have value (brand awareness, traffic, diversity)

content.text: Good vs. Bad Backlinks

Good backlinks are: editorial (earned, not bought), relevant (same topic), from diverse domains (not all from one source), and have natural anchor text. Bad backlinks are: paid links, private blog networks (PBNs), link farms, forum profile spam, and automated comment links.

items: Good example: A news site links to your research study using your brand name
Bad example: 'Buy backlinks' service adds your link to 500 low-quality directories
Google penalty: Manual action for unnatural links (check Google Search Console)
Recovery: Disavow bad links + removal requests

content.code:
# Simple backlink quality classifier
def classify_backlink(domain_authority, relevance_score, is_editorial, anchor_text):
    score = 0
    if domain_authority > 50: score += 3
    elif domain_authority > 30: score += 1
    if relevance_score > 7: score += 2
    if is_editorial: score += 3
    if anchor_text.lower() in ["click here", "read more"]: score -= 1
    if score >= 6: return "Good link"
    elif score >= 3: return "Neutral — monitor"
    else: return "Potentially toxic — consider disavow"

The Mom Test: Introduction & Overview

The Mom Test, coined by Rob Fitzpatrick, is a set of customer interview techniques that prevent you from being told reassuring lies. The core rule: Avoid asking about the future (people lie), hypotheticals (people guess), or opinions (people please). Instead, ask about specific past behaviors and facts.
Why 'Mom'? The Mom Trap

Your mom will always say your idea is great because she loves you, not because it's true. So will friends, polite strangers, and sometimes even potential customers who don't want to hurt your feelings. The Mom Test helps you get honest, actionable feedback by shifting from 'Would you buy this?' to 'When was the last time you tried to solve this?'

items: Bad question: 'Do you think this is a good idea?' → they say yes to be nice
Better: 'How do you currently handle X?' (past behavior)
Even better: 'What was the last problem you had with Y?' (specific)
Best: 'Show me how you did that last time' (observation)

content.alt: Mom Test vs. normal interview: lies vs. truths graph

rows: What do you think of this feature?
When did you last face this problem?
Can you walk me through your process?

content.title: Rob Fitzpatrick Explains The Mom Test (30 min keynote)

content.text: The 3 Golden Rules

Rule 1: Talk about their life, not your idea. Rule 2: Ask about specifics, not generalities. Rule 3: Listen more than you talk (80/20 rule). If you find yourself pitching or explaining, you're doing it wrong. Good interviews feel like a detective uncovering a timeline, not a sales call.

items: Anchor questions: 'Tell me about the last time you…', 'How much did that cost you in time/money?'
Avoid leading: 'Don't you hate when X happens?' → ask 'What frustrates you about X?'
Watch for non-verbal cues (long pauses, hedging language = likely not a real problem)

rows: Would you use a calendar app with AI? →
What's your current system for scheduling meetings?
Ignore prototype. Ask: What's the hardest part of your workflow?
Talks about their life, not your idea
When did you last exercise? How many times this week?

content.title: Live Mom Test Coaching Session (Bad vs. Good Interviewer) (28 min)

content.text: The 'Commitment' Test

After asking about past behavior, look for signs of real commitment. Ask: 'Would you be willing to be a beta tester?' or 'Can I send you an email when we launch?' or 'I'm looking for a case study — can we shadow you for an hour?' If they say yes without hesitation, that's a lead. If they say 'maybe later' or ghost, that's a no.

items: Level 1 commitment: 'That's interesting' (worthless)
Level 2: 'Send me more info' (low value, easy to say)
Level 3: 'I'll join your beta / give you 15 min of my time' (good)
Level 4: 'I'll pay a deposit / sign an LOI' (best signal)

content.code:
## Commitment Ask Script

After you've heard a real problem, try:

'That's really helpful. We're exploring a tool to help with [problem]. 
Would you be open to trying a rough prototype next month? 
I'd just need 20 minutes of your time for setup — no cost, no commitment beyond that.'

If they say yes: book a calendar invite immediately.
If they say no or hesitate: note that this is a weak signal problem.

content.text: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistake 1: Introducing your idea before asking questions (now they're biased to please). Fix: 'I'm not going to tell you what I'm working on yet — I just want to learn about your world.' Mistake 2: Interviewing only friendly people. Fix: Find 'anti-early adopters' who are skeptical. Mistake 3: Not recording interviews. Fix: Record (with permission) and transcribe. You'll catch what you missed.

items: Use the 'three-interview rule': after 3 interviews, stop and look for patterns
If you hear 'it depends' or 'sometimes' → you're not asking specifically enough
Keep a 'parking lot' for ideas you want to pitch — don't pitch during the interview

content.text: The Build-Measure-Learn Loop: Summary & Next Steps

The Build-Measure-Learn (BML) loop is the core feedback mechanism of the Lean Startup methodology. This summary module recaps the loop's phases, common failure modes, and provides a roadmap for integrating BML into your weekly product development cadence.
Recap: Build → Measure → Learn

Build: Turn an idea into a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) — the smallest thing that can test a hypothesis. Measure: Collect quantitative data (funnel metrics) and qualitative feedback (interviews). Learn: Decide to pivot or persevere. Speed around the loop is critical (aim for 1–2 week cycles).

items: Build: MVP ≠ product; it's an experiment (e.g., landing page, concierge service, fake door)
Measure: One metric that matters (e.g., activation rate, retention, or revenue per user)
Learn: Document the hypothesis before building (not after) to avoid confirmation bias

content.alt: BML loop diagram with pivot/persevere decision point

content.title: BML Loop in 5 Minutes (Animated Summary)

content.text: Common Failure Modes (How Loops Break)

Failure 1: Build phase takes months (big launch syndrome) → loop too slow. Failure 2: Measure phase uses unvalidated data (e.g., sample too small) → false learnings. Failure 3: Learn phase produces no clear decision → endless 'maybe' → morale drops. Failure 4: Skipping the loop entirely and just building.

items: Fix slow builds: break into weekly sprints with a shippable test each week
Fix bad data: set minimum sample size (e.g., 50 conversions or 100 interviews)
Fix indecision: use a 'pivot or persevere' calendar invite every 2 weeks — non-negotiable

content.alt: BML loop speed comparison: slow vs. fast cycles

content.title: Case Study: How Dropbox Used a Video MVP (BML in action) (26 min)

content.text: Next Steps: Weekly BML Cadence

Implement this weekly template: Monday 10 AM: Hypothesis review (what are we testing this week?). Tuesday–Wednesday: Build/run experiment. Thursday: Measure (pull data, user interviews). Friday 3 PM: Learning meeting (pivot/persevere decision for next week). Document each loop outcome in a BML log.

items: Step 1: Identify #1 risk (e.g., retention, activation, pricing)
Step 2: Form falsifiable hypothesis: 'If we [action], then [metric] will improve by [X]'
Step 3: Design MVP experiment (minimum code, maximum learning)
Step 4: Run experiment for exactly 1 week (no extending)
Step 5: Analyze and decide before Monday

**Date:** 2025-03-15
**Hypothesis:** Adding social proof testimonials on pricing page will increase conversion rate from 2% to 2.6% (30% lift).
**MVP:** Add 3 testimonials (existing customers, real names) via A/B test (50/50).
**Data:** Total visitors: 2,400 (control 1,200, variant 1,200). Control conversions: 24 (2.0%). Variant conversions: 33 (2.75%). Statistical significance: p=0.03.

content.text: Integrating with Other Frameworks

BML pairs with: (1) Value Proposition Canvas (to identify what to test), (2) Pirate Metrics (to know which stage of the funnel to focus experiments on), (3) The Mom Test (for qualitative learning). Use them together: VPC → BML → AARRR.

items: If you have no customers → do Mom Test interviews first, then BML
If you have low retention → BML experiments on onboarding
If you can't decide which metric → run an AARRR audit to find the leak

content.text: Conversion Tracking: Introduction & Overview

Conversion tracking is the process of measuring how many users complete a desired action (conversion) and which marketing channels drove them. This introductory module covers basic concepts: conversion rate, event tracking, pixel installation, and goal setup in Google Analytics.
What is a Conversion?

A conversion can be a purchase (macro), an email signup (micro), a video watch, or even a page scroll. Define your primary conversion first — the one that generates revenue or directly aligns with your business goal. Secondary conversions are leading indicators.

items: Examples: 'Thank you' page view, form submission, click-to-call button, account creation
Conversion rate = (conversions / sessions) × 100
Benchmark: ecommerce ~2-3%, B2B SaaS ~5-10% (free trial), lead gen ~10-15%

content.text: How Tracking Works (The Technical Side)

You place a tracking pixel (JavaScript snippet) on your site. When a user visits a page or clicks an element, the pixel sends an event to an analytics platform (Google Analytics, Facebook Pixel). The platform records the event, along with UTM parameters, user ID, timestamp, and other metadata.

items: Install base tracking code (e.g., gtag.js, Facebook Pixel) on all pages
Identify conversion action (e.g., visit /thankyou page)
Set up event or pageview goal in your analytics tool
Test in real-time to ensure firing
Wait 24-48 hours for data

content.text: Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Tracking only macro conversions (ignore micros → can't diagnose funnel). Mistake 2: Not including conversion value (e.g., order amount). Mistake 3: Using 'last-click' attribution without understanding its bias. Mistake 4: Not filtering internal traffic (your own team's visits skew data).

items: Fix #1: Set up 3-5 micro conversion goals (e.g., 'Add to cart', 'Initiate checkout')
Fix #2: Add dynamic conversion value via dataLayer (e.g., order total)
Fix #3: Compare last-click vs. first-click in an attribution report
Fix #4: Exclude IP addresses of your office/VPN in GA4 filters

content.text: The Mom Test: Summary & Next Steps

This module summarizes the key principles of The Mom Test and provides a practical roadmap for integrating its techniques into your product discovery process. You'll learn how to run a week of effective customer interviews and avoid the most common post-interview traps.
The Three Rules (Refresher)

Rule 1: Talk about their life, not your idea. Rule 2: Ask about specifics (past behavior, not generalities). Rule 3: Listen 80% of the time. If you break any rule, you'll likely hear polite lies. Print these rules and put them on your wall during every interview.

items: Rule 1 violation: 'What do you think of our prototype?' → Fix: 'Put that away, let's talk about your last project'
Rule 2 violation: 'How often do you typically...' → Fix: 'When was the last time you did X?'
Rule 3 violation: You talk >50% → Fix: Silence. Count to 5 after they finish speaking.

content.alt: Mom Test rules summarized in one visual poster

rows: Let me show you this feature
Walk me through your current workflow
When did you last struggle with X? What happened?
You're the one learning facts about them, not vice versa

content.title: 5 Minutes to a Better Interview (Roleplay Example)

content.text: The 3-Question Opening Script
Start every interview with these three open-ended questions. They establish trust and immediately get to past behavior without biasing the conversation toward your solution.

items: Q1: 'What does a typical [workday / week / project] look like for you?' (broad context)
Q2: 'What's the most frustrating part of that? Tell me about the last time it happened.' (pain discovery)
Q3: 'How have you tried to solve that so far?' (reveals existing solutions & effort)

content.code:
## Mom Test Interview Script (Cheat Sheet)

**Intro (30 sec):** "Thanks for your time. I won't pitch anything — I just want to understand how you currently handle [domain]."

**Core:**
1. "Walk me through the last time you [relevant activity]."
2. "What was the hardest part of that?"
3. "What did you try? Did anything help?"

**Commitment check:**
"If we build something to solve [problem], would you be open to a 15-min usability test next month?"

**Outro:** "That's all my questions. What should I have asked that I missed?"

content.text: Next Steps: A 5-Day Action Plan

Day 1: Identify 10 potential interviewees (target people who already experience the problem, not friends/family). Day 2: Write your script using the template above. Day 3: Conduct 3 practice interviews (recorded, with permission). Transcribe and highlight rule violations. Day 4: Revise script and do 5 real interviews. Day 5: Look for patterns across all 8 interviews. Do not build anything until you see the same problem mentioned by at least 5 people unprompted.

items: After interviews, create a spreadsheet: one row per user, columns for Problem, Existing solution, Severity (1-5)
Look for 'vivid language' — exact phrases users repeat (e.g., 'spreadsheet hell')
If you can't find 5 people with the same severe problem, your idea is likely not viable. Pivot or kill it.
Re-interview users with the problem after you build a paper prototype (still no code)

content.title: Case Study: A Startup That Did The Mom Test Wrong (Then Right) (33 min)

content.text: Common Post-Interview Biases

Confirmation bias: Remembering the one person who loved your idea and forgetting the 9 who were lukewarm. Fix: Write a summary immediately after each interview, before talking to teammates. Social bias: Teammates will also avoid criticizing. Fix: Have a 'devil's advocate' role in post-interview debriefs who only lists reasons to kill the idea.

items: Use the 'five whys' on any positive feedback: 'That's interesting — why do you say that?'
If they say 'I'd definitely use that', reply: 'What's stopping you from solving this with existing tools today?'
After 8 interviews, if no one offered to be a beta tester or give you a referral, the problem isn't painful enough.

content.text: Resources & Community

Read the full book: The Mom Test by Rob Fitzpatrick (free online with some licenses). Join the Mom Test Slack community for interview critiques. Use the Mom Test question bank (100+ validated questions) in the resources section. Your final exercise: Record a 5-minute interview with a stranger and submit for peer review.
The Dynamics of Change: Practical Frameworks

Organizational change fails 70% of the time, often due to resistance, poor communication, or lack of reinforcement. This module covers four evidence-based frameworks: Kotter's 8 Steps, ADKAR, Lewin's 3-Stage Model, and the Change Curve (Kübler-Ross adaptation for business).
Framework 1: Kotter's 8-Step Change Model

John Kotter's model starts with creating urgency before making any changes. Steps: (1) Create urgency, (2) Form coalition, (3) Vision, (4) Communicate, (5) Remove obstacles, (6) Short-term wins, (7) Build on change, (8) Anchor culture. Skipping steps leads to failure.

items: Step 1 example: Share customer churn data to show why change is urgent
Step 2 example: Enlist 3 respected leaders (not just top brass)
Step 3-4: 'We will reduce time-to-market by 40% in 6 months'
Step 5-6: Remove budget blocker, celebrate first milestone (e.g., first team adopts new tool)
Step 7-8: Promote change agents, update onboarding materials to reflect new culture

content.alt: Kotter's 8 steps infographic with ice metaphors

rows: Use real data (customer complaints, competitor moves)
Include middle managers and informal influencers

content.title: Kotter in Action: How a Hospital Reduced Wait Times (29 min)

content.text: Framework 2: ADKAR (Individual Change)

ADKAR focuses on the individual: Awareness (why change?), Desire (to participate), Knowledge (how to change), Ability (skills), Reinforcement (sustain). Use when you have resistance at the person-level. Ask: which letter is missing? Lack of Awareness = explain the why. Lack of Desire = address personal WIIFM.

items: A: 'The old system will be deprecated in 90 days'
D: 'Early adopters will receive extra training and recognition'
K: 'We'll hold daily 15-min workshops'
A: 'Practice environment available 24/7'
R: 'Quarterly bonuses tied to new process adoption'

rows: Why is this change needed? (1-5 scale)
Connect to career growth, reduce pain points

content.alt: ADKAR model diagram with barriers per stage

content.title: ADKAR in 15 Minutes (Case: ERP Implementation)

content.text: Framework 3: Lewin's 3-Stage (Unfreeze → Change → Refreeze)

Unfreeze: Break down existing mindsets (create psychological safety to question old ways). Change: Introduce new processes, tools, or behaviors. Refreeze: Embed changes into culture, policies, and rewards. Do not skip refreeze — otherwise people revert to old habits within weeks.

items: Unfreeze tactic: 'Lessons learned' session where it's safe to admit failures of old system
Change tactic: Pilot with volunteers first, then scaled
Refreeze tactic: Update employee handbooks, performance reviews, and Slack #announcements

content.code:
## Lewin's Model Checklist

**Unfreeze (Weeks 1-3)**
☐ Hold a 'state of the union' addressing why change is inevitable
☐ Acknowledge losses (old ways, status) to reduce defensiveness
☐ Stop legacy processes that conflict (remove old forms, disable old software)

**Change (Weeks 4-8)**
☐ Run parallel pilots (old + new) with 10% of teams
☐ Provide just-in-time support (office hours, chat channel)
☐ Celebrate early adopters publicly

**Refreeze (Weeks 9-12+)**
☐ Retire old system completely (no fallback)
☐ Update all documentation and training materials
☐ Link new process to performance reviews

rows: No one can articulate the old way's flaws

content.alt: Lewin's ice cube analogy (cube -> water -> new cube)

content.title: Change Curve: The Emotional Journey (18 min)

content.text: Choosing the Right Framework

Use Kotter for large-scale, top-down transformation (mergers, digital transformation). Use ADKAR for stubborn individual resistance or when you have low morale. Use Lewin when you need a simple visual for teams and can control the environment. Use the Change Curve (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) to understand emotions — especially in layoffs or relocations.

items: The most common mistake: starting with solution (Change phase) without Unfreezing
Measure change readiness using a survey (e.g., 'On a scale of 1-5, how ready are you?')
Assign a 'change champion' for every 20 employees for peer support

content.text: Exercise: Change Management Simulation

Scenario: Your company is moving from Slack to Teams (or similar tool). Resistance is high among senior engineers. Using Kotter: what's the urgency? Using ADKAR: which element is missing for engineers? Using Lewin: how do you unfreeze? Write a 2-paragraph change plan and test it with a colleague playing the resistant engineer.
Advanced Technique #1: Causal Inference with Difference-in-Differences

A/B tests aren't always possible (e.g., launching in one country). Difference-in-differences (DiD) compares the change over time in a treated group vs control group. Example: Launch feature in Germany (treatment), compare to France (control). Measure metric before and after for both, then (Germany_after - Germany_before) - (France_after - France_before) = causal impact. Requires parallel trends assumption.

content.caption: Treatment vs control before/after

items: Step 1: Identify treatment group (e.g., users who saw new feature) and control (similar, didn't)
Step 2: Measure metric for both groups pre- and post-
Step 3: Calculate difference in differences
Step 4: Test significance with regression

content.text: Advanced Technique #2: Synthetic Control for Macro Decisions

When no single control group exists, create a 'synthetic' control – weighted combination of many units that resembles treatment group before intervention. Example: Assess impact of a new pricing model in one region. Algorithm (e.g., Synthetic Control Method) finds weights for other regions to match pre-period. Compare post-period actual vs synthetic. Used by Google for YouTube ads impact.

rows: Single treated unit, many potential controls

content.code:
# Difference-in-differences regression
import statsmodels.formula.api as sm
df['post'] = (df['time'] >= treatment_date).astype(int)
df['treatment'] = (df['region'] == 'treatment').astype(int)
df['interaction'] = df['post'] * df['treatment']
model = sm.ols('metric ~ post + treatment + interaction', data=df).fit()
# Coefficient on 'interaction' = causal impact
print(f"Causal impact: {model.params['interaction']:.2f}")

content.title: Causal inference beyond A/B testing

content.text: Advanced Technique #3: Bayesian A/B Testing with Early Stopping

Frequentist A/B tests require fixed sample sizes; stopping early inflates false positives. Bayesian methods allow continuous monitoring: calculate probability that variant B > A. Stop when probability >95% (or <5%). Example: After 1,000 conversions, P(B > A) = 92% – continue. At 1,500, 97% – stop and rollout. Expected sample size reduction: 30-50%.

items: Prior: Beta(1,1) (uniform) for conversion rate
Posterior: Beta(conversions+1, trials-conversions+1)
Probability B > A = samples from posterior B > posterior A
Implement with PyMC or scipy.stats.beta

content.caption: Posterior distributions showing probability B beats A

content.text: Advanced Technique #4: Multi-Armed Bandit for Real-Time Optimization

Instead of A/B test followed by rollout, bandits allocate traffic dynamically to better-performing variants. Example: Epsilon-greedy – 90% traffic to best variant so far, 10% explore others. Thompson sampling – sample from posterior, allocate proportionally. Result: users see winning variant sooner, no 'test period' where 50% see bad variant. Used by Netflix, Amazon, LinkedIn.

content.title: Multi-armed bandits for real-time experimentation

content.text: Pitfall #1: Performative Empathy ('I Hear You' then Nothing)

Managers say 'I understand' but take no action. Empathy without action is manipulation. Example: Employee says 'I'm overwhelmed', manager says 'I hear you' – but assigns more work. Trust erodes. Fix: Always follow empathy with commitment: 'That sounds hard. What one thing could I take off your plate today?' Then do it. Action ratio: for every empathy statement, one tangible act within 24 hours.

content.caption: Empathy without action = betrayal

items: Step 1: Validate emotion ('That makes sense')
Step 2: Ask 'What would help right now?'
Step 3: Commit to one action ('I will...')
Step 4: Do it within 24 hours
Step 5: Follow up ('Did that help?')

content.text: Pitfall #2: Emotional Contagion (Absorbing the Emotion)

Empathetic managers absorb team's stress, leading to burnout. Example: Manager feels 'anxious' because team is anxious – now two anxious people, problem unsolved. Fix: Switch from 'emotional empathy' (feeling with) to 'cognitive empathy' (understanding without absorbing). Practice: label the emotion ('I see you're frustrated'), but don't take it on. Use perspective-taking: 'What are they experiencing? What do they need?'

content.code:
## Cognitive Empathy Script
**Employee**: 'I'm so stressed about this deadline.'
**Affective (bad)**: 'Oh no, now I'm stressed too.' (absorbs)
**Cognitive (good)**: 'I understand deadlines create pressure. Walk me through what's blocking you.'
**Compassionate (best)**: 'That sounds hard. Let's look at the timeline together – what can I adjust?'

content.title: How empathetic managers burn out (and how to stop)

content.text: Pitfall #3: Empathy Only for Direct Reports (Not Peers)

Managers often empathize down but not sideways. Peers feel unheard, collaboration suffers. Example: Product manager empathizes with engineers but not with marketing – marketing feels dismissed, delays happen. Fix: Apply empathy map to all stakeholders, not just your team. Before cross-functional meeting, ask: 'What pressures are they under? What's their win?'

items: Red flag: 'I don't have time to think about their problems'
Fix: Spend 5 min before each cross-functional meeting on stakeholder empathy
Example: Sales under quota pressure – frame requests in terms of 'how this helps them close deals'

content.caption: Extend empathy to peers, not just reports

rows: 'I know you need quick wins – here's a feature customers asked for'
'I understand cost scrutiny – let me show ROI model'
'I get you need to protect us – what's the least risky path?'

content.text: Pitfall #4: Assuming Empathy = Agreeing

You can empathize without agreeing. Example: 'I understand why you're frustrated with the policy' (empathy). 'But we have to follow it' (doesn't require agreement). Many managers avoid empathy because they fear it implies agreement. Fix: Separate validation from alignment. Use 'And' not 'But': 'I hear you, AND we still need to meet the deadline.'

content.code:
# Empathy without agreement template
def respond_with_empathy_and_boundary(employee_statement, boundary):
    empathy = f"I hear that you feel {employee_statement['emotion']} about {employee_statement['topic']}."
    boundary_statement = f"At the same time, {boundary}."
    invitation = "What's a way we could address both?"
    return f"{empathy} {boundary_statement} {invitation}"

# Example
print(respond_with_empathy_and_boundary(
    {'emotion': 'frustrated', 'topic': 'the new process'},
    'we need to follow it for compliance'
))
# Output: "I hear you're frustrated about the new process. At the same time, we need to follow it for compliance. What's a way we could address both?"

content.title: Empathy doesn't mean agreement: how to hold both

content.text: Advanced Technique #1: Agile at Scale – The Spotify Model Demystified

The 'Spotify Model' (Squads, Tribes, Chapters, Guilds) is a mental model, not a prescription. Advanced agile leaders adapt it: Squads (small teams, 6-8 people) own a mission. Tribes (10-100 people) are collections of squads. Chapters (functional guilds, e.g., frontend engineers) maintain standards. Guilds (communities of interest) share knowledge. Key: Don't copy blindly – adapt to your size. For <50 people: squads + chapters only. >100: add tribes.

content.caption: Squads, tribes, chapters, guilds

items: Squad: cross-functional, mission-driven, autonomous
Chapter: same skill (e.g., QA) across squads
Tribe: up to 10 squads, same business area
Guild: voluntary interest group (e.g., AI enthusiasts)

content.text: Advanced Technique #2: The Agile Fluency Model

Not every team needs 'advanced agile'. Agile Fluency model has 4 zones: Zone 1 (Focus on value) – teams deliver on spec, need strong product owners. Zone 2 (Deliver market) – teams own roadmap, deploy frequently. Zone 3 (Optimize value) – teams run experiments, measure outcomes. Zone 4 (Innovate) – teams invent new markets. Most teams should aim for Zone 2. Zone 4 requires exceptional talent and low regulation.

content.code:
## Agile Fluency Self-Assessment
**Zone 1 (Focus on value)**: [ ] We deliver what we committed [ ] Stakeholders trust us
**Zone 2 (Deliver market)**: [ ] We deploy weekly [ ] We get user feedback within days
**Zone 3 (Optimize value)**: [ ] We run experiments [ ] We measure outcomes, not output
**Zone 4 (Innovate)**: [ ] We create new categories [ ] We have a 'disrupt or die' mandate
Goal: reach Zone 2 for 80% of teams

content.title: Agile fluency model: what level do you need?

content.text: Advanced Technique #3: Team Topologies (Conway's Law Management)

Conway's Law: systems mirror communication structures. Change your team structure to change your architecture. Team Topologies defines 4 team types: Stream-aligned (customer-facing), Platform (internal services), Enabling (help others learn), Complicated-subsystem (specialist). Also interaction modes: Collaboration (working together), X-as-a-Service (API), Facilitating (coaching). Design teams, then architecture follows.

items: Stream-aligned: owns a business capability (e.g., 'Checkout squad')
Platform: provides internal APIs (e.g., 'Auth platform')
Enabling: helps stream-aligned adopt new tech
Complicated-subsystem: deep expertise (e.g., 'Recommendation engine')

content.caption: 4 team types and 3 interaction modes

content.text: Advanced Technique #4: Strategic Agile Metrics (North Star + Balance)

Beyond velocity (output), measure outcomes: deployment frequency, lead time to deploy, mean time to recover (MTTR), change fail rate. For agile health: employee NPS, team autonomy score (how many decisions can team make without approval?). For business: time from idea to cash (TIIC). Balance leading (deployment frequency) and lagging (customer NPS). Set goals: e.g., 'deploy daily' not 'more story points'.

content.title: Moving beyond velocity: advanced agile metrics

content.text: Core Concept #1: The Johari Window – Your Blind Spot

The Johari Window divides self-knowledge into four quadrants: Open (known to self and others), Blind (known to others, not self), Hidden (known to self, not others), Unknown (unknown to both). Core concept: leadership effectiveness correlates with size of the 'Open' area. Grow it by: asking for feedback (shrinks Blind) and self-disclosure (shrinks Hidden).

content.caption: Four quadrants of self-awareness

items: Open: 'I know I'm good at strategy, and my team agrees'
Blind: 'I interrupt, but I don't notice' (team does)
Hidden: 'I'm anxious about this project' (I know, team doesn't)
Unknown: 'I thrive in chaos' (neither knows yet)

content.text: Core Concept #2: The Ladder of Inference (How We Jump to Conclusions)

We observe data → select data → add meaning → make assumptions → draw conclusions → adopt beliefs → take actions. This happens in milliseconds. Self-awareness requires climbing down the ladder: (1) What's the observable data? (2) What meaning did I add? (3) What assumption am I making? (4) What's another interpretation? Used to reduce conflict.

rows: 'She didn't reply to my email for 2 days'
I notice only the late reply, not her 20 replies last week

**Step 5 – More helpful belief**: ______

content.title: Climbing down the ladder of inference

content.text: Core Concept #3: The Two Types of Self-Awareness (Internal & External)

Internal self-awareness: how clearly you see your own values, passions, aspirations, fit with environment. External self-awareness: how clearly you see how others see you. They are independent – you can have high internal, low external (e.g., 'I know I'm funny, but others find me annoying'). Research: high external self-awareness predicts leadership effectiveness more than internal.

items: Internal: 'I value autonomy' (self-perception)
External: 'My team thinks I'm micromanaging' (others' perception)
Gap between internal and external = blind spot
Action: Ask 5 people 'What's one thing I could do more of? Less of?'

content.caption: High external awareness = better leader

content.text: Core Concept #4: The Weekly Reflection Habit (5 Questions)

Build self-awareness with a 10-min weekly reflection. Questions: (1) What went well this week? (2) What was challenging? (3) What did I learn about myself? (4) What will I do differently next week? (5) What feedback will I seek? Do it Friday afternoon. After one month, review patterns. Top self-aware leaders do this without fail – it's a discipline, not inspiration.

content.text: Practical Framework #1: The OKRs Playbook (One-Pager)

OKRs = Objectives (qualitative, inspirational) + Key Results (quantitative, 2-5 per objective). Example: Objective 'Delight customers'. KRs: 'Reduce support tickets by 20%', 'Increase NPS from 45 to 55', 'Launch customer advisory board'. Rules: 3-5 objectives max per company. KRs must be measurable (0-100%). Score at quarter end: 70% is success (stretch). Not tied to compensation (or people hide stretch).

content.caption: One-page OKR playbook

items: Step 1: Write 3 company objectives (aligned to strategy)
Step 2: Write 2-5 KRs per objective (output-focused, not tasks)
Step 3: Cascade to teams (each team has 3 objectives aligned to company)
Step 4: Review weekly, score monthly
Step 5: Retro at quarter end – what blocked KRs?

content.text: Practical Framework #2: The Strategy Canvas (Blue Ocean)

A strategy canvas plots your offering vs competitors across key factors (price, quality, features, service). Blue Ocean strategy: eliminate (factors taken for granted), reduce (below standard), raise (above standard), create (new factors). Example: Cirque du Soleil eliminated animals, stars; created theme, artistry. Framework: Draw current canvas (industry standard), then draw your 'to-be' canvas – where do you eliminate, reduce, raise, create?

content.text: Practical Framework #3: The Ansoff Matrix (Growth Strategy)

2x2 grid: Markets (Existing/New) x Products (Existing/New). Four strategies: Market Penetration (existing/existing) – low risk. Product Development (new product/existing market) – medium. Market Development (existing product/new market) – medium. Diversification (new/new) – high risk. Framework: plot your growth initiatives. 70% of resources to Market Penetration, 20% to Product/Market Development, 10% to Diversification (70-20-10 rule).

items: Market Penetration: sell more to current customers (e.g., loyalty program)
Product Development: new product for current customers (e.g., new feature)
Market Development: current product to new segment (e.g., international)
Diversification: new product to new market (e.g., acquihire)

content.caption: Risk increases diagonally

content.text: Practical Framework #4: The 3 Horizons of Growth

Horizon 1: core business (extend and defend) – 70% of resources. Horizon 2: emerging opportunities (build new streams) – 20% of resources. Horizon 3: long-term bets (explore, maybe fail) – 10% of resources. Framework: list all initiatives, assign to H1/H2/H3. If H2+H3 < 20% of resources, you're under-investing in future. Review quarterly. Example: Amazon – AWS started as H3, became H1.

content.title: The 3 horizons of growth (McKinsey framework)

content.text: What is Automation Architecture? A Definition

Automation architecture is the design of systems that execute repetitive tasks without human intervention. It includes triggers (time, event, API call), logic (if-then, workflows), actions (email, API update, database write), and monitoring. Introduction covers: event-driven vs time-driven, idempotency, error handling, and observability. Good automation is reliable, auditable, and recoverable.

content.caption: Trigger → Logic → Action → Monitor

items: Trigger: Scheduled (cron), Event (webhook), Polling (check every X min)
Logic: Conditional, loop, data transformation
Action: API call, email, database, message queue
Monitor: Logs, alerts, dead-letter queue

content.text: Why Automation Architecture Matters (Even for Small Teams)

Without architecture, you get 'spaghetti automation' – fragile scripts on laptops, manual recovery, no audit trail. Example: A marketing automation script ran on a manager's laptop; when they went on vacation, lead flow stopped. Fix: Move to cloud functions (AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions) with logging, retries, and alerts. Start with low-code tools (Zapier, Make) but migrate to code when complexity grows.

content.code:
# Minimal viable automation architecture
from fastapi import FastAPI, BackgroundTasks
import logging

app = FastAPI()

def process_webhook(data):
    try:
        # Business logic here
        logging.info(f"Processing {data}")
    except Exception as e:
        logging.error(f"Failed: {e}")
        # Send to dead-letter queue
        send_to_dlq(data)

@app.post("/webhook")
async def webhook(data: dict, background_tasks: BackgroundTasks):
    background_tasks.add_task(process_webhook, data)
    return {"status": "accepted"}  # Acknowledge immediately

content.title: Automation architecture for non-engineers

content.text: Key Design Patterns for Automation

Pattern #1: Idempotent operations – running twice produces same result (use unique IDs, check before action). Pattern #2: Retry with backoff – exponential backoff for transient failures. Pattern #3: Circuit breaker – stop calling failing API after 5 failures. Pattern #4: Dead-letter queue – save failed messages for manual inspection. Without these, automation fails silently.

items: Idempotency: 'If email already sent, skip'
Retry: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s up to 5 times
Circuit breaker: Open after 5 failures, reset after 60s
DLQ: Store in S3 or database with timestamp

content.caption: Idempotency, retry, circuit breaker, DLQ

rows: Store in persistent queue for manual review

content.text: Observability: Logging, Metrics, Alerts

Automation must be observable. Log each invocation: start, end, error. Metrics: success rate, latency, volume. Alerts: if success rate <95% for 5 min, page on-call. Example: Zapier has basic logs; custom automation use DataDog, Sentry, or self-hosted (Prometheus + Grafana). Start with structured logging (JSON) from day one – enables searching.

content.title: Monitoring automation: logs, metrics, alerts

content.text: Why Strategic Frameworks? (Introduction)

Strategic frameworks are mental models that simplify complex decisions. They answer: Where to play? How to win? What capabilities? What management systems? Without frameworks, strategy is guesswork. Introduction covers three foundational frameworks: Porter's Five Forces (industry attractiveness), SWOT (internal/external), and PESTEL (macro environment).

content.caption: Frameworks reduce complexity

items: Porter's Five Forces: rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, supplier power, buyer power
SWOT: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats
PESTEL: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal

content.text: When to Use Which Framework

Use Porter's Five Forces when entering a new industry or analyzing competition. Use SWOT at the start of strategy offsite (30 min). Use PESTEL for long-term (3-5 year) planning or international expansion. Don't use SWOT alone – it's descriptive, not prescriptive. Combine with Porter to identify 'what to do about threats/opportunities'.

content.text: Common Mistakes with Strategic Frameworks

Mistake #1: Using SWOT without action – 'We have a strength in brand' so what? Fix: convert each SWOT factor into a strategic initiative. Mistake #2: Treating Porter's Five Forces as static – industries change quarterly. Mistake #3: Overcomplicating – you don't need 10 frameworks. Pick 3 max. Mistake #4: Frameworks instead of data – they organize thinking, but you need market data to populate them.

items: Action: After SWOT, write 'Because of X strength, we will Y'
Action: Re-run Porter's Five Forces every 6 months
Rule: Use a framework only if it changes a decision – otherwise it's theater

content.text: Practical Framework #1: The AARRR Funnel Audit (2-Hour Exercise)

Run a 2-hour funnel audit with your team. Step 1: Map current state conversion rates (e.g., 10k visits → 1k signups (10%) → 200 activated (20%) → 50 retained D30 (25%) → 10 referrals (20%) → $5k revenue ($500 per user). Step 2: Identify biggest drop-off (largest % loss). Step 3: Brainstorm 3 experiments for that stage. Step 4: Assign owner and due date. Repeat monthly.

content.caption: Find the biggest leak

items: Acquisition to Activation: biggest drop? (e.g., 10% signup rate)
Activation to Retention: next biggest? (e.g., 25% D7 retention)
Prioritize: fix biggest drop first (80/20 rule)

content.text: Practical Framework #2: The LTV/CAC Dashboard

Track LTV (Lifetime Value) and CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost) by channel. LTV = ARPU × gross margin × (1 / churn). CAC = total marketing spend / customers acquired. Target ratio: LTV/CAC > 3x. If <3x, reduce CAC or increase LTV. If >5x, you're under-investing in growth. Build dashboard: channel, CAC, LTV, ratio, spend. Update monthly.

content.text: Practical Framework #3: The North Star Metric Workshop

North Star Metric = single metric that best predicts long-term success. For Spotify: time listened. For Airbnb: nights booked. For Slack: messages sent. Workshop: (1) List candidate metrics (2) Test: does it capture value delivered to customer? (3) Test: is it a leading indicator of revenue? (4) Vote. Output: North Star + 3-5 input metrics (e.g., for Spotify – playlists created, shares, new artists discovered).

items: Bad North Stars: revenue (lagging), MAU (can be inactive)
Good: 'weekly active teams' (Slack), 'rides completed' (Uber)
Pro tip: measure at user level, not aggregate

content.text: Practical Framework #4: Cohort Retention Table (Template)

Build a cohort retention table in Google Sheets: rows = signup month (e.g., Jan 2025), columns = week 0,1,2,3,4. Cell = % still active. Format as heatmap (green=high retention, red=low). Identify which cohorts underperform (e.g., Feb cohort worse than Jan) and investigate (marketing source? onboarding change?). Update monthly. Look for improving or declining trend.

content.code:
-- Cohort retention query (PostgreSQL)
WITH cohorts AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    DATE_TRUNC('month', signup_date) AS cohort_month,
    DATE_TRUNC('week', activity_date) - DATE_TRUNC('week', signup_date) AS weeks_since_signup
  FROM user_activity
)
SELECT 
  cohort_month,
  weeks_since_signup,
  COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) / MAX(COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)) OVER (PARTITION BY cohort_month) AS retention_rate
FROM cohorts
WHERE weeks_since_signup BETWEEN 0 AND 12
GROUP BY cohort_month, weeks_since_signup
ORDER BY cohort_month, weeks_since_signup;

content.text: Practical Framework #1: The EAST Framework (Behavioral Economics)

EAST (Easy, Attractive, Social, Timely) from UK Behavioural Insights Team. Easy: reduce friction (defaults, remove steps). Attractive: grab attention (loss aversion, personalization). Social: show peer behavior (testimonials, live activity). Timely: when they're most receptive (after a win, before a deadline). Use EAST to design product features, emails, and user flows.

content.caption: Easy, Attractive, Social, Timely

items: Easy: Set default to opt-in (e.g., automatically enroll in trial)
Attractive: Highlight what they'll lose, not gain ('Don't lose your streak')
Social: 'Join 50k others who already upgraded'
Timely: Ask for review immediately after a win

MINDSPACE: Messenger (who communicates), Incentives (rewards/punishment), Norms (what others do), Defaults (pre-set options), Salience (what stands out), Priming (subconscious cues), Affect (emotion), Commitment (public promises), Ego (self-image). Use as checklist for any user touchpoint. Example: 'We'll donate $1 for every signup' (Incentives + Ego).

content.text: Practical Framework #3: The COM-B Model (Capability, Opportunity, Motivation)

Behavior change requires all three: Capability (physical/psychological ability), Opportunity (external factors), Motivation (automatic/reflective drive). If a behavior isn't happening, diagnose which is missing. Example: Users don't complete onboarding. Capability? (too hard). Opportunity? (too long). Motivation? (no reward). Fix accordingly. COM-B is more diagnostic than EAST.

items: Capability: Do they know how? Is it too complex? Fix: simplify, guide
Opportunity: Is the environment enabling? Time? Social? Fix: reminders, social support
Motivation: Do they want to? Habits? Beliefs? Fix: incentives, feedback

content.caption: All three needed for behavior change

rows: Move task to mobile, reduce steps, async

content.text: Practical Framework #4: The Behavior Change Wheel (BCW)

BCW maps interventions to COM-B. Intervention types: Education, Persuasion, Incentivization, Coercion, Training, Restriction, Environmental restructuring, Modeling, Enablement. Pick based on diagnosis. Example: Low Capability? Training, Enablement. Low Motivation? Incentivization, Persuasion. Low Opportunity? Environmental restructuring. Apply to reduce churn, increase signups, drive referrals.

content.text: Pitfall #1: Brand Story Without Customer as Hero

Many brand stories cast the company as hero (we saved the day!). But great stories cast the customer as hero, company as guide (like Yoda to Luke). Example: Apple's 'Think Different' celebrated users (heroes), not Apple's engineering. Fix: Use 'Hero's Journey' framework: customer has problem (call to adventure), meets guide (you), gains tools (your product), wins. Your brand appears only as guide.

content.caption: Customer = hero. Brand = guide.

items: Bad story: 'We built a better mousetrap'
Good story: 'You struggled with mice. We gave you the tool. You conquered.'
Test: Count 'we/our' vs 'you/your' in your story. Should be 1:3 ratio

content.text: Pitfall #2: Story That's Not True (Greenwashing, Overpromise)

When brand story doesn't match reality, customers detect it. Example: 'We care about the environment' but packaging is plastic. 'We're innovative' but product hasn't updated in 2 years. Fix: Audit your story against product, hiring, operations. If there's a gap, either change the story or change the company. Authenticity > polish. Patagonia's 'Don't buy this jacket' story works because it's true.

rows: Reduce hold times or change story

## Brand Story Truth Audit
**Our brand promise**: ______
**Evidence we deliver**: ______
**Evidence we contradict**: ______
**Gap severity (1-10)**: ______
**If gap >5**: Either fix the operations or soften the story.
**If gap <3**: Amplify the story – it's authentic.

content.title: Closing the brand story vs reality gap

content.text: Pitfall #3: Too Many Characters, No Clear Plot

Brand stories with multiple protagonists (customers, founders, employees, investors) confuse audiences. Or plot holes: 'We help you X, also Y, also Z' – no through-line. Fix: One protagonist (customer segment). One plot (problem → solution). One antagonist (old way, competitor). Supporting characters appear only to advance plot. Example: Dove's 'Real Beauty' – protagonist (real women), antagonist (unrealistic beauty standards), plot (self-esteem).

items: Step 1: Who is your single protagonist? (e.g., 'busy parent')
Step 2: What is their single biggest problem? (e.g., 'no time for healthy meals')
Step 3: What is the antagonist? (e.g., 'fast food', 'time poverty')
Step 4: What is the plot? (e.g., 'from overwhelmed to in control')

content.caption: One protagonist, one antagonist, one plot

rows: We help you be more productive

content.text: Pitfall #4: Forgetting the Audience's 'Why Should I Care?'

Stories that focus on brand's history ('Founded in 2010...') bore audiences. Opening must answer 'Why should I care within 5 seconds?'. Fix: Start with customer pain, not brand origin. 'Remember when you wasted 2 hours on [problem]?' not 'We launched in 2020 with a mission to...'. Hook = shared pain or aspiration. Then introduce your role as guide. Save history for 'About Us' page, not homepage.

content.text: Value Proposition Design: Practical Frameworks

Moving beyond theory, this module provides three practical, repeatable frameworks for designing, testing, and iterating your value proposition: the Value Proposition Canvas (VPC), the Value Proposition Matrix, and the 5-Step Testing Loop. You'll leave with templates you can apply tomorrow.
Framework 1: The Value Proposition Canvas (Strategyzer)

The VPC has two sides: Customer Profile (Jobs, Pains, Gains) and Value Map (Products, Pain Relievers, Gain Creators). Fit occurs when each pain reliever addresses a specific customer pain, and each gain creator delivers a specific gain. Use sticky notes — physical or digital — and iterate rapidly.

items: Step 1: List 5-10 functional jobs (e.g., 'organize receipts'), 3-5 emotional jobs ('feel in control of finances'), 2-3 social jobs ('look professional to clients')
Step 2: Identify 5-7 pains (e.g., 'losing receipts', 'manual data entry takes hours')
Step 3: Identify 3-5 gains (e.g., 'automatic tax categorization', 'real-time expense reports')
Step 4: Map your product features to pain relievers (e.g., 'OCR scanning' relieves 'manual entry')
Step 5: Identify orphaned pains/gains — these become your product roadmap

content.alt: Value Proposition Canvas blank template with labels

rows: Manual entry, lost receipts, no audit trail

content.title: Filling the VPC: Live Workshop (35 min)

content.text: Framework 2: The Value Proposition Matrix (Prioritization)

Not all value drivers are equal. Use a 2x2 matrix: Impact (low-high) vs. Uniqueness (low-high). Quadrants: (1) High Impact + High Uniqueness = Core differentiator (invest heavily). (2) High Impact + Low Uniqueness = Table stakes (must have). (3) Low Impact + High Uniqueness = Nice-to-have (deprioritize). (4) Low Impact + Low Uniqueness = Remove.

items: Example (Zoom): High Impact + High Uniqueness = 'Virtual background' (in 2020)
Table stakes = 'HD video' (everyone has it now)
Nice-to-have = 'Whiteboard' (low usage)
Remove = 'Built-in games' (distracting, low impact)

content.alt: Value Proposition Matrix quadrant chart with examples

content.title: How to Kill Low-Value Features (Case: Trello) (22 min)

content.text: Framework 3: The 5-Step Testing Loop

After designing your VPC, test each hypothesis before building. Step 1: State hypothesis (e.g., 'Small business owners will pay $20/month to automate receipt scanning'). Step 2: Design minimal test (e.g., landing page with 'Buy now' button). Step 3: Run test with 30-50 target customers. Step 4: Measure (e.g., 10% clicked 'buy' = success). Step 5: Decide to keep, tweak, or discard.

items: Hypothesis template: 'We believe that [customer segment] will [action] because [reason]'
Minimal test types: smoke test (landing page), concierge (do manually), fake door (button leads to 'coming soon')
Success metric: Must be quantitative (e.g., 20% conversion, not 'positive feedback')
Timebox: 1-2 weeks maximum. If you can't test in 2 weeks, break into smaller sub-hypotheses.

content.text: Common Pitfalls & How to Avoid Them

Pitfall 1: Filling VPC from internal assumptions instead of customer interviews. Fix: Do 5 Mom Test interviews before touching sticky notes. Pitfall 2: Including too many jobs/pains/gains (analysis paralysis). Fix: Limit to 7 per category. Pitfall 3: Testing everything at once. Fix: Test one pain reliever per week.

items: Red flag: Your VPC has no emotional or social jobs (means you don't understand motivation)
Red flag: Every pain reliever links to multiple pains (too vague)
Red flag: Your testing loop has no numeric success criterion

content.code:
# VPC health check
def vpc_health(customer_profile, value_map):
    issues = []
    if len(customer_profile['jobs']) < 5:
        issues.append("Too few jobs — may miss important use cases")
    if len(value_map['pain_relievers']) > len(customer_profile['pains']):
        issues.append("More pain relievers than pains — overbuilding")
    # Check each pain reliever maps to at least one pain
    unmapped = [pr for pr in value_map['pain_relievers'] 
                if not any(pr.lower() in pain.lower() for pain in customer_profile['pains'])]
    if unmapped:
        issues.append(f"Unmapped pain relievers: {unmapped}")
    return issues if issues else "VPC is fit"

print(vpc_health({'jobs': ['a','b'], 'pains': ['slow']}, {'pain_relievers': ['fast', 'cheap']}))

The Pirate Metrics (AARRR): Summary & Next Steps

This module summarizes the AARRR framework (Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Revenue, Referral) and provides a roadmap for applying it to your startup or product. You'll learn how to audit your funnel, prioritize leaks, and set weekly AARRR goals.
Recap: The 5 Metrics That Matter

Acquisition: How users find you. Activation: First 'Aha!' moment. Retention: Do they come back? Revenue: Monetization. Referral: Do they bring others? Each stage has a conversion rate; multiply them to get end-to-end funnel conversion. Focus on the worst-performing stage first.

items: Acquisition: Cost per acquisition (CPA), channel mix, CTR
Activation: % who complete key action (e.g., upload file)
Retention: Day 1, 7, 30 retention; churn rate
Revenue: Average revenue per user (ARPU), LTV, payback period
Referral: Net Promoter Score (NPS), viral coefficient (K)

rows: Test new channels; improve landing page

content.text: The AARRR Audit: Step-by-Step

Perform a weekly 30-minute AARRR audit. Step 1: Export last 30 days of data from analytics (GA4, Mixpanel, or your DB). Step 2: Calculate rate for each stage. Step 3: Order stages by worst to best conversion. Step 4: Identify the single biggest drop (e.g., 40% to 10% retention). Step 5: Propose one experiment to improve that stage for next week.

items: Use cohort analysis (not aggregate) for retention — group users by signup week
For early-stage (pre-product-market fit), ignore acquisition and focus on activation + retention
Set up an automated dashboard (e.g., in Google Looker Studio) to see AARRR live

content.code:
-- AARRR query example (PostgreSQL)
WITH acquisition AS (
  SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) as acquired
  FROM sessions WHERE date >= NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
),
activation AS (
  SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) as activated
  FROM events WHERE event_name = 'did_core_action' 
    AND date >= NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
),
retention AS (
  SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) as retained
  FROM sessions WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM signups WHERE week = 1)
    AND date BETWEEN NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days' AND NOW()
)
SELECT 
  a.acquired,
  ac.activated,
  ROUND(100.0 * ac.activated / a.acquired, 1) as activation_rate_pct,
  r.retained,
  ROUND(100.0 * r.retained / ac.activated, 1) as retention_rate_pct
FROM acquisition a, activation ac, retention r;
